page: Google Cloud Platform c3d-standard-60 is a general-purpose compute instance built on the x86_64 architecture and powered by an AMD EPYC 9B14 processor. The configuration provisions 60 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 30 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. It provides 240 GB of system memory, matching a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM allocation with 4 GB per virtual core. Cache infrastructure consists of 32 KB of L1 data cache, 1 MB of L2 cache, and 32 MB of L3 cache. Instruction set extensions include AVX-512 variants (f, vnni, bf16) alongside cryptographic accelerators like VAES and SHA_NI. The instance includes neither bundled local NVMe storage nor hardware GPU acceleration.

Benchmark evaluation shows top-tier computational density across multi-threaded scenarios. The platform scores 86123.9 on stress-ng multi-core tests, 68156.01 on PassMark CPU, and 17809.0 on Geekbench multi-core. Parallel tasks such as Clang software compilation and ray tracing demonstrate high execution speeds. The memory architecture achieves 78.31 million Redis SET operations per second and strong performance in database operations testing. In contrast, uncached memory bandwidth measures at moderate levels (145.23 GB/s read, 52.23 GB/s write), indicating that data processing scales best when working within cache hierarchies.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the balanced CPU-to-memory ratio avoids the resource premiums of specialized memory-heavy or GPU tiers. The omission of local storage avoids base pricing overhead for stateless infrastructure relying on networked volumes. The instance is suited for multi-threaded application servers, CI/CD compilation farms, distributed database nodes, and CPU-based machine learning inference pipelines.

Equipped with AVX-512 and cryptographic instruction sets, it exhibits high multi-core throughput across stress-ng, PassMark CPU, and software compilation benchmarks. This profile aligns directly with CI/CD build environments, large-scale backend services, in-memory caching layers, and CPU-driven inference workloads.
